sentences.gloss_en: Welcome to this explainer.
Today we go on a really fun trip inside the complex details of the backend.
We will trace, exactly step by step, the journey of any request from the moment it leaves the client until it dives deep into the database and comes back.
It is not just a straight line, not at all.
It is a journey full of bumps and technical details you will really like.
Let us quickly look at our roadmap: we will go through six stations.
First, the request journey and the language wars; second, we look at some (unclear) in Java and the Streams.
Third, JDBC and transactions; fourth, we stop at the connection pool; fifth, the Spring Boot layers.
And finally we close with concurrency and the saga pattern.
Great, let us start with our first station.
The request journey and the language wars that always go on in this layer.
Picture with me the spatial map of the request.
It first knocks on the door of the Controller, which receives it and routes it.
Then it goes down to the Service, which holds all the business rules.
From there to the Repository, which writes the SQL, until we reach the connection pool and finally the database.
The core idea here is that all these layers depend on each other vertically.
So if any small problem happens in the connection pool, everything above stops completely and the whole system goes down.
Now look at this direct comparison between Python and Java doing the same task; it is really interesting.
Python gives you very short code, about 20 lines, with dynamic typing.
But at the same time it is constrained by something called the GIL.
On the other side, Java code can reach 80 lines or more.
But it makes up for it with static typing that catches errors very early.
And it runs on the JVM with a JIT compiler that gives tremendous speed.
And most important of all: true multithreading.
When we build systems handling billions of records at production scale, this architecture makes a huge difference.
Based on that, let us go inside the Service layer and uncover some hidden programming traps in Java.
Here we have a really clever trap that can catch anyone.
If we write Integer 127 == 127 in code, the result is true, as expected.
But if we write Integer 128 == 128, the result suddenly becomes false. How?
The whole secret is the Integer cache: the JVM pre-stores numbers from -128 to 127.
So any == comparison between them succeeds.
But 128 is treated as a completely new object in memory.
So the golden rule to avoid disasters in code: always use .equals in comparisons instead of the == sign.
And the Java Streams API works brilliantly, exactly like the equivalent of pandas in Python.
We can chain operations one after another very easily, like filter, map, groupingBy and sum, with the same power and flexibility.
Another trap: if you use a parallel stream on small data sets, performance gets slower, not faster as you imagine.
That is because the cost of splitting the work across threads is bigger than the execution time itself.
Now let us go a bit deeper to the Repository layer, specifically the third station: the JDBC journey and transactions.
The steps here are clear and very direct.
We open the connection, then create a PreparedStatement, execute the query, and walk through the results via the ResultSet.
But focus with me: the most important step of all here is the PreparedStatement.
Why? Because it completely blocks any SQL injection attacks, since it separates the data from the code entirely.
We also use try-with-resources to close the connection automatically so no resources leak.
Here comes the real transaction action: we turn off auto commit and start the scenario.
We insert a new order and try to deduct from stock, but we add a very smart condition.
If that condition is not met and the stock was not enough, the whole operation stops and we roll back immediately.
That rollback is like turning time back, as if the order never happened at all.
And it fully protects us from race condition problems if several orders come in at the same moment.
The fourth station we are reaching now is the very critical infrastructure: the connection pool.
See this number 10?
It is not just a number; it is the maximum number of connections in a config like HikariCP, for example.
Imagine this scenario: 10 connections, all checked out and busy with other requests.
Suddenly request number 11 arrives; what does it do? Wait in a queue?
If the timeout passes without any connection freeing up...
Boom, we hit a dead-end wall and get a fatal error called pool exhausted.
At that moment the whole system is paralyzed, simply because there is no way out to the database.
To spare ourselves writing all this manual work every time, we move to the fifth station: the Spring Boot layers.
Here we see the real magic of Spring Boot: how it wraps the whole journey we described with just simple annotations.
We put @Entity to describe the table, and use JpaRepository so it writes the queries for us.
And we put @Service with @Transactional to handle the business rules and rollbacks elegantly.
And finally @RestController for API routing.
Ordered, organized layers that connect each step with minimal effort.
But watch out: this ease comes with responsibility, and traps too.
The great thing here is the GlobalExceptionHandler, a central place that unifies the responses.
It returns 404 if something is not found, 409 if there is a conflict, or 500 as an internal error.
But the truly scary trap is the JPA N+1 query trap, caused by a feature called lazy loading.
If we have, say, 100 records, instead of one query the system runs a main query and then 100 sub-queries, one per record.
That is 101 queries just for 100 records.
Can you imagine how this destroys performance?
Now we reach the climax of our explainer: the sixth station, concurrency and the saga pattern.
Comparing concurrency, Python relies on a few tricks: threading for I/O, multiprocessing for CPU, or asyncio.
All of that is to work around the limits of the GIL.
But in Java it is different: we are talking about true multi-core multithreading.
Threads really run on several cores at the same moment.
Of course this power is not free: it needs great caution and strict protection of shared data using atomic safety, so no interference happens.
When the work grows and is spread over several microservices, each with its own database, a single transaction and a normal rollback no longer work.
Here a hero called the saga pattern appears.
The idea is we move forward: reserve stock, then pay.
But if the shipping step hits a problem and fails, we run the reverse operations in reverse order, what we call compensation.
That is, refund the money first, then cancel the stock reservation.
This is the only way to guarantee consistency in these complex distributed systems.
After this whole tour, from the connection pool to the saga pattern and compensating operations, an important question arises.
How can we manage all these complex, distributed data pipelines reliably at enterprise scale?
How do we make sure everything happens on time and in the right order?
That is exactly the question that opens the door to exploring the world of ETLs and DAGs in the next stage.
The condition read aloud: where stock is greater than or equal to question mark.
